title: Not All Modern Exotic Cars Are Hot Right Now

body_markdown:
Whether you’re an obsessive market-watcher like us or just a casual observer of how collector cars are selling, over the past 10 months you’ve probably seen some version of the “exotic cars are hot” headline. Hypercars are selling for hyper-prices. Modern Ferraris are defying all logic and breaking price guides. High-spec Porsches basically don’t depreciate.


And some of the numbers really are crazy. The[Porsche Carrera GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/carrera_gt/2004/2004-porsche-carrera_gt-base?id=aCn1I000000DV8tSAG) cost about $400K when it was new, barely 20 years ago. Now, it’s a $3M car.[Ferrari Enzos](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/enzo/2003/2003-ferrari-enzo-base?id=aCn1I000000DI6oSAG) started at about $700K. Several have sold for eight figures in 2026. Diablos and Murciélagos have notably appreciated this year, and Bugatti Veyrons are up 28% since January. So it’s easy to assume that everything with the engine in the middle, low production numbers, and a fancy name is having a graph-go-up year. But not so fast. There are several modern exotics, even ultra-exclusive ones, for which the rational laws of automotive depreciation are still applying.


Mecum


A somewhat surprising one is the McLaren Speedtail. It debuted in late 2018, and McLaren billed it as a sort of spiritual successor to the F1, complete with the same central driving position and even an identical production run of 106 cars, in the Speedtail’s case roughly $2.5M. Today, a McLaren F1 can cost 10 times that amount, so big demand for the supposedly similar but much cheaper Speedtail might have made sense.


And the first few that did hit the open market did sell for strong, though not excessive, money. Since 2022, though, Speedtails sold publicly haven’t done anything to write home about.


Broad Arrow


Both the Sián FKP 37 and Countach LPI 800-4 are hybrid V-12s based on the Aventador with ultra-exclusive production numbers (82 for the Sián, 112 for the Countach) that sold out almost immediately. Production of both wrapped up in 2022, and both had price tags in the multi-million-dollar range. Both look wild, even by Lamborghini standards.


Now that a few years have passed, people aren’t exactly throwing their checkbooks at these low-production Lambos. Even as other modern V-12 Lamborghinis—including Aventadors—are selling above their original MSRPs, the Sián and the resurrected Countach just aren’t.


From late 2021 to late 2024, Aston Martin sold 275 examples of its hybrid hypercar, the Valkyrie. Packed with Formula One tech and looking like a street-legal Le Mans car, it still hasn’t done anything particularly surprising in an auction setting, aside from one sale of a rare Spider model for[$4.735M](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo26/lots/v0001-2024-aston-martin-valkyrie-spider/) back in August. Other Astons have experienced much worse depreciation.


The sample sizes above are admittedly small, but they’re small for all the big exotic car market winners of 2026, too. Many of those market winners are Ferraris, which also makes us wonder if the company’s famous allocation system for new models is pushing up prices for the older ones. Maybe, and that’s a topic for further discussion, but Ferraris aren’t the only big gainers this year, and there are even winners and losers within the same brand, like the Lamborghinis above, or the[Ford GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ford+gt) . Prices for the 2005–06 models are up 42% this year. For the 2017–22 model, they’re flat as a pancake. We’ve often called the market “mixed” this year, and this is true even in the exotic car corner.
